nameStory: The bumblebee millipede gets its cheerful name from its striking yellow and black banded pattern that looks remarkably like a bumblebee's fuzzy stripes. This eye-catching coloration serves as a warning to predators — just like a bee's colors say 'stay away,' the millipede's bright bands advertise that it can release foul-smelling defensive chemicals when threatened.
description: The bumblebee millipede is a colorful, cylindrical arthropod that looks like a living piece of striped jewelry crawling through the leaf litter. Its body features alternating bands of bright yellow and dark brown or black, creating a distinctive pattern that's hard to mistake for any other millipede. These tropical visitors typically reach 2-4 inches in length and have dozens of tiny legs that move in wave-like motions as they explore their surroundings. Unlike their native New England cousins, bumblebee millipedes are occasional exotic escapees or hitchhikers from warmer climates.

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Bright yellow bands alternating with dark brown or black stripes around the entire body, creating a vivid bumblebee-like appearance that's visible even from several feet away

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Perfectly cylindrical body that feels firm and smooth to the touch, like a flexible pencil, with distinct segments visible as rings around the circumference

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Notably larger than most native New England millipedes, typically 2-4 inches long and about the thickness of a marker or small cigar

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Moves with characteristic millipede wave-motion of legs, but appears more robust and deliberate than native species, often curling into a tight spiral when disturbed

idTips.label: Defensive Behavior
idTips.description: When threatened, releases a strong, acrid chemical smell that's much more pungent than native millipedes and may cause temporary skin irritation if handled

habitat: In New England, bumblebee millipedes are extremely rare and typically found only around greenhouses, botanical gardens, or homes with tropical plant collections where they may have arrived as stowaways in imported soil or plants. They require warm, humid conditions and rich organic matter, so any sightings would likely be in heated spaces, compost piles near heated buildings, or temporarily in warm outdoor mulch during summer months.

seasonality.spring: Unlikely to be seen outdoors; any sightings would be in heated greenhouses or indoor plant collections where they remain active year-round.
seasonality.summer: Most likely season for outdoor sightings, particularly in warm compost piles, mulched garden beds, or areas with rich organic soil near buildings.
seasonality.fall: May occasionally be spotted in warm microhabitats like compost or mulch piles, but will seek shelter as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Only found in heated indoor spaces like greenhouses, conservatories, or homes with large plant collections.

funFact: This tropical millipede can actually glow under ultraviolet light, fluorescing with a ghostly blue-green color that scientists think may help them recognize their own species in the dark forest floors of their native Caribbean homes.
confusionNotes: The bright yellow and black banding makes this nearly impossible to confuse with any native New England millipede, which are typically uniform brown, gray, or reddish. If you see a striped millipede in New England, you've likely found something very unusual that doesn't belong here naturally.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'bumblebee millipede,' this species is completely unrelated to bees and poses no stinging threat — the name refers only to its similar color pattern. Finding one in New England would be noteworthy enough to report to local naturalists, as established populations this far north would be quite remarkable.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus recorded in New England, the bumblebee millipede stands out dramatically from all native species due to its tropical origins and striking coloration. While New England has several native millipede species in different families, none display anything close to the vivid yellow and black banding of this Caribbean visitor. The closest visual comparison might be to some large centipedes, but millipedes move much more slowly and have far more legs per body segment.
